question.knowledge_point: Finding the Coefficient of a Particular Term
question.problem: The coefficient of ${x}^{12}$ in the expansion of ${(2+x)}^{15}$ is
question.worked_solution:
The binomial theorem states that for any positive integer $n,$ we have

$$
(a+b)^{n}=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{0}){a}^{n}{b}^{0}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{1}){a}^{n-1}{b}^{1}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{2}){a}^{n-2}{b}^{2}+⋯+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{n}){a}^{0}{b}^{n}.
$$

In the case of ${(2+x)}^{15},$ we have $a=2,$ $b=x,$ and $n=15.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}(2+x)^{15}=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{15}{0}){2}^{15}{x}^{0}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{15}{1}){2}^{15-1}{x}^{1}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{15}{2}){2}^{15-2}{x}^{2}+⋯+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{15}{15}){2}^{15-15}{x}^{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

From here, we see that the ${x}^{12}$ term must be

$$
(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{15}{12}){2}^{15-12}{x}^{12}.
$$

Evaluating the coefficient, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{15}{12}){2}^{15-12} & =455\cdot {2}^{3} \\  & =455\cdot 8 \\  & =3\,640.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coefficient of ${x}^{12}$ is $3\,640.$

question.knowledge_point: Solving Trigonometric Equations Involving Cosecant Under a Modified Domain
question.problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=2$ for $-\pi \le x<\pi ,$ what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},$ therefore the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

First, we have to find the principal value:

$$
x=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{\pi }{6}.
$$

Since $\frac{\pi }{6}$ lies in the required domain, the first solution is ${x}_{1}=\frac{\pi }{6}.$

Our first solution lies in the first quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{6}.$ Since $\operatorname{sin}⁡x>0,$ the second solution must lie in the second quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{6}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13989101/assets/00d540b1f6412e4af2617452fbf0c58750d01e844d89d0d92cfacc0cb3e45e32.png)

Since the second solution lies in the $2$nd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi -\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{5\pi }{6}.$

Finally,

$$
\frac{\pi }{6}\cdot \frac{5\pi }{6}=\frac{5{\pi }^{2}}{36}.
$$

question.problem:
Which of the following equations has no solutions for $0\le x<2\pi ?$

I. $\operatorname{csc}⁡x+30=4\operatorname{csc}⁡x$

II. $5\operatorname{csc}⁡x-1=2\operatorname{csc}⁡x$

III. $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=4\operatorname{csc}⁡x-12$
question.worked_solution:
We first simplify the given equations, and get

I. $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=10$

II. $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{3}$

III. $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=4$

Now, recall that the range of $\operatorname{csc}⁡x$ for $0\le x<2\pi $ is given by

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡x\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ).
$$

So, the equation $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=k$ has no solutions for $k\in (-1,1).$ 

Therefore, of the given equations, only equation II has no solutions.

question.knowledge_point: Finding an Entry of the Product of Two Matrices
question.problem:
Let $R=PQ.$ What is the value of ${r}_{25}$, if

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 3 & -4 \\ 4 & -6 \\ 1 & -8 \\ 3 & -9\end{aligned}],\,Q=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 & -1 & 10 \\ 2 & 0 & 5 & -2 & 7\end{aligned}]?
$$
question.worked_solution:
Multiplying the $2$nd row of $P$ by the $5$th column of $Q$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{25} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 3 & -4 \\ 4 & -6 \\ 1 & -8 \\ 3 & -9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 & -1 & 10 \\ 2 & 0 & 5 & -2 & 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}10 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =3\cdot 10+(-4)\cdot 7 \\  & =30-28 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Multiplying a Column-Vector By a Row-Vector
question.worked_solution:
Here, $A$ is $3\times 1$ matrix and $B$ is a $1\times 2$ matrix. 

There is $1$ column in matrix $A$ and $1$ row in matrix $B$, so the product is well defined:

$$
{A}_{3\times \boxed{\text{1}}}{\cdot }_{✓}{B}_{\boxed{\text{1}}\times 2}={AB}_{3\times 2}
$$

Computing the product, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0\cdot 1 & 0\cdot 2 \\ (-2)\cdot 1 & (-2)\cdot 2 \\ (-3)\cdot 1 & (-3)\cdot 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -2 & -4 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Solving a Trigonometric Equation Involving Secant with Non-Special Angles
question.problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=-\frac{7}{2}$ for ${0}^{∘}\le x<{360}^{∘},$ what is the numerical value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2},$ rounded to the nearest integer?
question.worked_solution:
Recall that $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x},$ therefore the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡x=-\frac{2}{7}.
$$

First, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{arccos}⁡(-\frac{2}{7})=106.601\,549{…}^{∘}≈{106.602}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${106.602}^{∘}$ lies inside the required domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}={106.602}^{∘}.$

Our first solution lies in the second quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}={73.398}^{∘}.$ Since $\operatorname{cos}⁡x<0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}={73.398}^{∘}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13989949/assets/e378560486eca17f870b21743718c9f984f2bd3bf5609601f1cea674e15018e6.png)

Since the second solution ${x}_{2}$ lies in the $3$rd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={180}^{∘}+{\theta }_{R} \\  & ={180}^{∘}+{73.398}^{∘} \\  & ={253.398}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=106.602\cdot 253.398≈27\,013,
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

question.knowledge_point: Finding a Quadratic Polynomial Given a Double Root and a Leading Coefficient
question.problem: The quadratic polynomial $P(y)$ has the double root ${y}_{1}={y}_{2}=3,$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $a=3.$ Find $P(y).$
question.worked_solution:
Since our quadratic polynomial has the double root ${y}_{1}={y}_{2}=3,$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $a=3,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(y-{y}_{1})^{2} & =3{(y-3)}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{(y-3)}^{2} & =3({y}^{2}-6y+9) \\  & =3{y}^{2}-18y+27.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P(y)=3{y}^{2}-18y+27.$

question.problem: The quadratic polynomial $f(v)$ has real coefficients, has roots ${v}_{1}=3+4\text{i}$ and ${v}_{2}=3-4\text{i},$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $2.$ Find $f(v).$
question.worked_solution:
Since our quadratic polynomial has roots ${v}_{1}=3+4\text{i}$ and ${v}_{2}=3-4\text{i},$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $a=2,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(v-{v}_{1})(v-{v}_{2}) & =2(v-(3+4\text{i}))(v-(3-4\text{i}))\end{aligned}
$$

Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2(v-(3+4\text{i}))(v-(3-4\text{i})) & =2({v}^{2}-(3+4\text{i})v-(3-4\text{i})v+(3+4\text{i})(3-4\text{i})) \\  & =2({v}^{2}-(3+4\text{i}+3-4\text{i})v+({3}^{2}-{4}^{2}{\text{i}}^{2})) \\  & =2({v}^{2}-6v+(9+16)) \\  & =2{v}^{2}-12v+50.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(v)=2{v}^{2}-12v+50.$

Consider the linear transformation $T$ with matrix representation $T,$ given by

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ is shown above. Which of the following is $\overset{―}{{A}^{′}{B}^{′}},$ the image of $\overset{―}{AB}$ under the action of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
To find the image of $\overset{―}{AB}$ under the action of $T$, we first create a matrix $X$ containing the coordinates of the endpoints of $\overset{―}{AB}:$

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we compute the image of $X$ under the action of $T$ by calculating the matrix product $TX:$

$$
\begin{aligned}TX & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -9 \\ 7 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the respective endpoints of the image are ${A}^{′}(5,7)$ and ${B}^{′}(-9,-3),$ as shown below.

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the image of $T$ under the action of $T$, we first create a matrix $X$ containing all of the vertices of $△ABC:$

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}]

$$
\begin{aligned}TX & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 & -3 \\ 4 & -6 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the respective vertices of $△{A}^{′}{B}^{′}{C}^{′}$ are $(6,4),(1,-6),(-3,2)$, as shown below.
